body:
One of the main things this is aiming to fix is the coupling, as we should ideally only have `main`/`platform` scripts referencing `main`, but `Performance` is referenced as early as `servers`. It's also registered during the `core` level of setup, albeit towards the end, so it felt most at-home in `core`

With that said, if we want to keep this as a "fix" to encapsulation while still keeping the scope reasonable, we could always just migrate this code to `servers/performance` instead. That'd still be encapsulated as expected, and would arguably be *more* fitting than assigning it to `core` (in its current form)

Which kind of coupling are you looking to fix with the PR?

The reason i was arguing about `Performance` not being subject agnostic is the potential knowledge violation: if `Performance` has knowledge of the rest of the codebase (rendering, navigation, etc.) it is not a reusable piece of data, which is the kind of thing `core` holds. Even if you eliminate include or call dependency violations, the _knowledge_ violation is what concerns me most, and it isn't addressed by this PR. Worse, if you eliminate the superficial dependencies, but keep the knowledge dependencies, you're effectively hiding them as silent coupling, which makes the code bug prone.

I understand the desire to avoid include / call layer violations (though we're currently pretty bad at this), but the one that we do have (`profiling.h` including `performance.h`, which I unfortunately missed during review...) isn't the kind of thing I would fix with the PR at hand. Otherwise, include and call dependencies look fine as-is to me.

I care much more about the include/dependency violations on paper, which might come from how much of my work is rooted in the buildsystem. The concept of a knowledge violation is an interesting one, but not necessarily one I'd consider a problem for `Performance`, as it's already setup such that it can receive and track arbitrary metrics. This function pointer dependency structure is already used in many places around the codebase, so while an argument can be made for it not being an ideal implementation, there *is* precedent for the approach

While I'd prefer a well-scoped and documented knowledge violation than a structurally flawed structural violation, I would wholeheartedly agree that neither approach is ideal. In reality, we should aim for a system that is designed with our envisioned encapsulation from the outset, rather than attempting to retrofit a system that's simply not suited for decoupling

> I'm not sure you answered my question yet as to where you see the problem with `Performance` being in `main` currently, and how this PR reduces that coupling? 

It's not an inherent problem; by all accounts, the location itself isn't the issue. The problem is when the intended encapsulation of the engine is broken by scripts outside of `main/` or `platforms/<selected_platform>/` referencing it. Full-stop, that's my only concern. By making `Performance` a core class instead, all those references are no longer a concern; though, that passes the buck to `Performance` as the referenced stats from other classes are now outside `Core`; this then was alleviated via pointer method calls.

An alternative implementation would be to make the classes that currently reference `Performance` to have pointer methods instead. However, cases like `editor/debugger/editor_performance_profiler.h` have methods that call the `MonitorType` enum instead, which means that would warrant some level of core/server level api that exposes `Performance` enums as well as pointer functions. But at that point, why not just make `Performance` a core/server class instead?

Not being engine-agnostic isn't a blocker in my eyes either, as we already have `core/config/` classes that are explicitly designed *for* the engine. Those scripts are utilized throughout `core/` and other non-`main/` scripts, much like `Performance` is.
